conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospital doctors. You came in with a lot of blood in your stool—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up early this morning—well, yesterday morning now—and had a really big bowel movement, mostly blood. It scared me, but I thought it might stop on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did it stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I had nine more episodes throughout the day. By the time I came in, I was dizzy and felt weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your blood count was low—27, down from 34.8 just two days ago. We gave you one unit of blood, but it didn’t go up, so we gave a second. You’ve had more bleeding today too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four more. Mostly blood, some clots. No pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve stopped your Plavix for now. You’re still on aspirin, but we’re watching closely. We’re concerned about your heart, so we paused your beta-blocker too, but you’ve been tachycardic—heart racing—so we restarted it this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel my heart racing when I sat up. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we monitor. With blood loss, your body tries to compensate by increasing heart rate. We want to keep you stable. You only have one IV, so we’re moving you to the ICU to get better access and watch you more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: ICU? That sounds serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a precaution. We want to make sure you don’t have more bleeding and that we can respond quickly if needed. You’re stable now, but we need to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without more bleeding. The team placed a central line in your neck yesterday—right internal jugular—for better access. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot, no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt the line placement, but it wasn’t too bad. Is the bleeding over?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new episodes since last night, which is a good sign. Today, you’re scheduled for a colonoscopy to look for the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy is done. We saw internal hemorrhoids and some diverticula in the sigmoid colon, but the rest of the colon looked normal—no active bleeding or signs of Crohn’s flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just hemorrhoids? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The bleeding pattern—maroon blood, large volume—could fit. But we can’t be certain. Since your blood count didn’t improve with transfusions, we’re concerned there might be another source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another source? Like where?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly higher up in the small intestine. We’re going to consult GI again and consider a capsule endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on the medical floor. No more bleeding overnight. Your hemoglobin is stable above 27. We’ve held your aspirin and Plavix for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need those for my heart, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but with active bleeding, they increase risk. We’ll restart them once we’re sure you’re stable. For now, we’re focusing on finding the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your aspirin this morning. You’ll stay on close watch. Your Crohn’s meds—Asacol and Cipro—are continuing. Insulin adjusted to 30 units at night since you’re eating less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Lantus 68 units. Is 30 enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. Your sugars are running 130–160, which is safe. As you eat more, you’ll need to increase it. Talk to your PCP to go back to 68 units at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have an update. After restarting aspirin, you had one more episode of bloody stool yesterday. We’ve held aspirin again and GI is reconsulting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean it’s coming from my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. They can increase bleeding risk. We’re scheduling a capsule endoscopy tomorrow to check your small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. The capsule endoscopy is complete. No active bleeding seen in the small intestine. You’ve had no more bloody stools since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So where was it coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still don’t have a definite source. Hemorrhoids are the most likely, but we can’t rule out a small, intermittent bleed. Your blood count is stable, so we’re confident you’re not actively bleeding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. You’ll follow up with your GI doctor. For today, we’re giving one more unit of blood because of your heart history, even though your levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m feeling better—no dizziness or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, no pain, hemoglobin steady. We’ll remove the central line this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stop aspirin, Plavix, and Diovan for now. Take Toprol at 25 mg instead of 100 mg until you see your cardiologist. Lasix only if your weight goes above 195 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue 30 units at bedtime for now. As you eat more, contact your doctor to increase back to 68 units.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What symptoms should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor if you have bloody stools, black tarry stools, chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. Otherwise, follow up with your GI and cardiology doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mom had colon cancer. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. You’ve had a normal colonoscopy in the past, and this episode may not be related. But keep up with screening as recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Creon for my pancreas. Should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue four capsules with meals. Same with Asacol, Cipro, and your other regular meds unless instructed otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue Neurontin, lidocaine patch, and Topamax. Use oxycodone or Oxycodone only as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad I’m going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll remove the central line, and a nurse will go over your discharge instructions. Feel free to ask any last questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—can I drive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right away. Wait until you’re off strong pain meds and feel steady. Have someone help you the first few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The central line has been removed. No bleeding at the site. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions. Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to schedule those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Let your doctors know if you have any issues before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for the next few days. Rest and follow the diet as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. No heavy lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Avoid straining. And keep an eye on your weight and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you.
